modules.title: Capital Structure and Sources of Finance
modules.html:
Types of Capital

TermMeaning
Authorised/nominal capitalMaximum a company may raise, stated in the memorandum
Issued capitalPart of authorised capital offered to the public
Called-up capitalPart of issued capital shareholders have been asked to pay
Paid-up capitalAmount actually paid by shareholders
Circulating/working capitalFunds for day-to-day operations
Fixed capitalLong-lived assets: land, buildings, machinery
Owner's equity/capital ownedTotal assets − total liabilities

Key Formulae

$$\text{Working Capital} = \text{Current Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Employed} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Current Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Capital Owned} = \text{Total Assets} - \text{Total Liabilities}$$ $$\text{Current Ratio} = \dfrac{\text{Current Assets}}{\text{Current Liabilities}}$$

Sources of Business Finance

  • Short term – bank overdraft, trade credit, factoring, commercial paper.
  • Medium term – term loans, hire purchase, leasing, equipment finance.
  • Long term – ordinary and preference shares, debentures, bonds, mortgage loans, retained earnings, venture capital, government/development bank loans.

Choice depends on cost, duration of need, security available, control implications and repayment ability.

examples.q: A firm has current assets ₦9,200,000, current liabilities ₦3,700,000 and total assets ₦28,000,000 with long-term loans of ₦7,000,000. Compute working capital, capital employed, capital owned and the current ratio.
Which source of finance suits (i) buying a delivery van (ii) paying staff salaries in a slow month?
examples.a: (i) A medium-term hire purchase or lease matches the van's life and spreads the cost; the asset itself serves as security. (ii) A bank overdraft is best – it is short term, flexible and interest is charged only on the amount actually used.

modules.title: Business Management and Organisation
modules.html:
Elements of Management (POSDCORB / Fayol)

  1. Planning – deciding objectives and how to achieve them.
  2. Organising – arranging resources and assigning duties.
  3. Staffing – recruitment, selection, training and remuneration.
  4. Directing/Leading – guiding and motivating employees.
  5. Co-ordinating – harmonising the work of departments.
  6. Controlling – measuring performance against standards and correcting deviations.
  7. Budgeting and reporting.

Principles of Management

Division of work, authority and responsibility, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain, span of control, delegation, discipline, remuneration, esprit de corps.

Departments of a Business

DepartmentMain duties
PurchasingSourcing suppliers, ordering, stock control
ProductionManufacturing, quality control, maintenance
Marketing/SalesMarket research, promotion, distribution, after-sales
Finance/AccountsRecords, budgets, payments, financial reporting
Human resourcesRecruitment, training, welfare, industrial relations
Administration/LegalCorrespondence, compliance, contracts

Organisational Structures

  • Line – direct vertical authority; simple and quick.
  • Line and staff – line managers advised by specialists.
  • Functional – authority by specialisation.
  • Matrix/committee – cross-functional project teams.

Span of control is the number of subordinates one manager can effectively supervise; a narrow span produces a tall structure, a wide span a flat one.

examples.q: A company of 240 workers uses a span of control of 6. How many first-line supervisors are needed, and what is the effect of widening the span to 12?
examples.a: At a span of 6: \( \dfrac{240}{6} = 40 \) supervisors. At 12: \( \dfrac{240}{12} = 20 \) supervisors. Widening the span halves supervisory cost and flattens the structure, but each supervisor now oversees more staff, so control and coaching may suffer.

examples.q: Explain 'unity of command' and give one consequence of breaking it.
examples.a: Each employee should receive instructions from only one superior. Where two managers give conflicting orders, the worker becomes confused, discipline breaks down, accountability is blurred and productivity falls.

modules.title: Legal Aspects of Business
modules.html:
Contract

A contract is an agreement enforceable by law. Essential elements:

  1. Offer and acceptance
  2. Consideration – something of value exchanged
  3. Intention to create legal relations
  4. Capacity – parties must be of age and sound mind
  5. Free consent – no fraud, duress, undue influence or misrepresentation
  6. Legality of object and possibility of performance

Contracts are discharged by performance, agreement, frustration, breach or operation of law. Remedies for breach: damages, specific performance, injunction, rescission and quantum meruit.

Sale of Goods

  • Condition – a vital term; breach allows rejection of the goods.
  • Warranty – a minor term; breach gives damages only.
  • Caveat emptor – ‘let the buyer beware’, now limited by implied terms of merchantable quality and fitness for purpose.
  • Nemo dat quod non habet – no one can give a better title than he has.

Agency

An agent acts on behalf of a principal to create legal relations with third parties. Created by express/implied appointment, necessity, estoppel or ratification. Duties of an agent: obey instructions, act in person, exercise care, account for money and avoid conflicts of interest. Terminated by performance, mutual agreement, revocation, death, insanity or bankruptcy.

Modern Trends and Ethics

E-commerce, mobile payment, outsourcing, franchising, corporate social responsibility, data protection (NDPC) and anti-money-laundering compliance now shape business practice. Ethical conduct – honest advertising, fair pricing, prompt tax payment and safe products – builds sustainable goodwill.

examples.q: Chika advertises a phone for ₦180,000 in a shop window. Musa insists the shop must sell at that price. Is he right?
examples.a: No. A shop display or advertisement is an invitation to treat, not an offer. Musa's willingness to pay is the offer; the shop may accept or reject it. Only on acceptance does a binding contract arise.

examples.q: A trader buys a generator described as 'brand new' but it turns out to be refurbished. State his remedy.
examples.a: The description goes to the root of the contract, so it is a condition, not a warranty. He may repudiate the contract, reject the generator and recover his money, and additionally claim damages for any loss suffered from the misdescription.

quiz.q: Which is a short-term source of finance?
quiz.solution: An overdraft is repayable on demand and used for temporary shortfalls.

quiz.q: Buying a machine on instalments while using it immediately is
quiz.solution: Under hire purchase the buyer uses the asset and owns it after the final instalment.

quiz.q: The number of subordinates a manager can effectively supervise is the
quiz.solution: Span of control determines whether a structure is tall or flat.

quiz.q: Unity of command means an employee should receive orders from
quiz.solution: Multiple bosses create confusion and conflicting instructions.

quiz.q: Which is NOT an element of a valid contract?
quiz.solution: An advertisement is usually only an invitation to treat, not an essential element.

quiz.q: Breach of a condition in a sale of goods entitles the buyer to
quiz.solution: A condition goes to the root of the contract, so the buyer may repudiate it.
The buyer should examine goods, though implied statutory terms now protect him.

quiz.q: A person who acts on behalf of another to make contracts is a(n)
quiz.solution: An agent creates legal relations between the principal and third parties.

quiz.q: Which department handles recruitment and training?
quiz.solution: HR manages staffing, welfare and industrial relations.
